title: Delhi High Court: NEET NRI Quota Can't Demand Guardianship Proof From Adult Candidates
excerpt: Justice Jasmeet Singh held the Guardians and Wards Act applies to minors — and questioned the MCC's demand that NRI sponsors prove they "looked after" students as a subjective, case-by-case hurdle.
body:
• The Delhi High Court has prima facie held that NEET-UG candidates seeking admission under the NRI quota cannot be asked to produce a legal guardianship certificate under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, if they are already 18 or older.
  • Justice Jasmeet Singh observed that the 1890 Act deals with minors and those caring for minors, and its provisions "do not seem to apply to persons who are aged 18 and above."
  • The ruling follows an earlier interim order questioning the Medical Counselling Committee's May 27 notification, which required NRI sponsors to prove they had "looked after" the student as a guardian — a "subjective criterion," the court said.
  • For now, an affidavit from the NRI sponsor plus documentary proof of financial capacity is enough to participate in NRI-quota counselling, keeping the 15% quota accessible to genuine applicants.

NEW DELHI — The Delhi High Court has pushed back against the Medical Counselling Committee's tightening of NRI-quota rules for medical admissions, holding that adult NEET-UG candidates cannot be forced to produce a court-ordered guardianship certificate for their NRI sponsors. Justice Jasmeet Singh observed that the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, deals with minors — and its provisions "do not seem to apply to persons who are aged 18 and above."

The case before the court

The plea was filed by a NEET-UG 2026 qualified candidate seeking admission to medical courses under the 15% NRI quota. She was sponsored by her maternal uncle — an Overseas Citizen of India/NRI settled in Australia and her nearest relative — who had substantially supported her after her father's death in 2023 and had always treated her as his ward. Her documents were rejected on the counselling portal because she had not uploaded a court order showing her sponsor was her legal guardian.

She challenged the MCC's notification of May 27, 2026, which required NRI-quota candidates to produce evidence demonstrating that the sponsor had acted as their guardian, along with an affidavit to that effect. The MCC's eligibility framework defines the "nearest relation" narrowly — real uncles and aunts, grandparents and first-degree cousins who are NRIs ordinarily residing abroad — and the May notification added the requirement of evidential proof of guardianship under the 1890 Act.

"A subjective criterion"

The latest ruling builds on an interim order the same judge passed on September 8, in which the court questioned the requirement that an NRI sponsor establish they had actually "looked after" the student as a guardian. Justice Singh said the condition "appears to introduce a subjective criterion, the satisfaction of which may vary from case to case." In that case — a minor candidate, Anish Sandeep Patil, sponsored by his NRI maternal uncle Shailesh Ashokrao Patil — the court directed authorities to let the candidate participate in the ongoing second round of counselling (then underway from September 3 to 9) on the strength of a sponsor's affidavit and documentary proof of financial capacity.

"The requirement appears to introduce a subjective criterion, the satisfaction of which may vary from case to case."

— Justice Jasmeet Singh, Delhi High Court

The Union of India had opposed interim relief, arguing the guardianship requirement was a safeguard against manufactured or bogus NRI claims and that court intervention could disturb the counselling schedule. The court acknowledged the concern but held it should, prima facie, be confined to ensuring admissions are not secured on false documents — not extended into judging the quality of a sponsor's relationship with the student.

Why this matters for NRI families

The NRI quota — 15% of seats in participating medical colleges — is a critical pathway for the children and wards of Indians abroad, and its fees run far higher than regular seats, which is precisely why the MCC tightened documentation to keep out ineligible applicants. But the May 27 notification landed just before counselling, leaving genuine families scrambling for court guardianship orders — a slow, expensive process — or locked out entirely. The court's interim position restores a workable standard: a sworn affidavit from the sponsor and evidence they can pay the fees.

What to watch

Both orders are prima facie findings at the interim stage, not final judgments — the court will decide the underlying challenge to the May 27 notification in full in the coming months. For families in the current counselling cycle, the practical takeaway is clear: if the sponsor is a genuine nearest relative with documented financial capacity, a missing guardianship certificate should not be the reason a seat is lost. Applicants turned away on that ground now have a court order to point to.
